title: Gukesh and Team India Stranded Five Hours Over Samarkand Hotel Chaos
excerpt: Captain Srinath Narayanan slammed the FIDE arrangements on X after the defending champions landed to find no rooms and no answers, a day before the Olympiad begins.
body:
• The Indian chess contingent, including world champion D Gukesh, was left stranded for five hours at Samarkand airport after landing in Uzbekistan for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, with no hotel rooms allotted.
  • Non-playing captain Srinath Narayanan took to X to flag the "terrible experience," writing there was "absolutely no clarity" on when rooms would be allotted; GM Vidit Gujrathi called it "very poor first impressions."
  • The episode comes a day before play begins on September 16, with India arriving as defending champions in both the Open and Women's sections after the historic double gold at Budapest 2024.
  • India fields a formidable Open squad — Arjun Erigaisi, R Praggnanandhaa, Nihal Sarin, Gukesh and Gujrathi — chasing a title defence no country has managed since Armenia in 2006-08.

The Indian chess team's arrival in Samarkand for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad turned into a five-hour ordeal on Tuesday, as the contingent — world champion D Gukesh included — was left waiting at the airport with no hotel rooms allotted and no word on when the situation would be resolved.

Grandmaster Srinath Narayanan, the non-playing captain of the men's team, broke the story on social media. "Having a terrible experience at the @FIDE_chess 2026 Olympiad. The team landed 5 hours ago at Samarkand airport," he posted on X. "The team still haven't been allotted rooms, with absolutely no clarity on when it'll be allotted."

GM Vidit Gujrathi, part of the playing squad, added his voice: "Very poor first impressions of the Samarkand, Uzbekistan Olympiad 2026. Still waiting…"

A rough start for the defending champions

The timing could hardly be worse. Play begins on Wednesday, September 16, and India arrives as the team to beat — defending champions in both the Open and Women's sections after the historic double gold at Budapest 2024, when both squads won their respective titles.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=AwFaO9GArdQ

Nearly 200 national teams are competing across the Open and Women's sections at the Silk Road International Exhibition Centre, with the tournament running through September 27. The Open top seeds are defending champion India, the United States — which brings the much-discussed Hans Niemann into the fray — host Uzbekistan, China and Germany. Notably absent from the marquee names are Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura and Alireza Firouzja.

"Having a terrible experience at the @FIDE_chess 2026 Olympiad. The team landed 5 hours ago at Samarkand airport. The team still haven't been allotted rooms, with absolutely no clarity on when it'll be allotted."

— GM Srinath Narayanan, India captain, on X

A squad built for a repeat

India's Open line-up is formidable. Arjun Erigaisi (2759) heads the team on board one, with R Praggnanandhaa (2750) on board two, Nihal Sarin (2718) on three, reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju (2703) on four, and Vidit Gujrathi (2697) on five. At Budapest 2024, Gukesh won individual gold as India finished four match points clear of the field, and Arjun took individual gold on board three.

https://x.com/ivyasaa/status/2099874322106216881

The women's team is equally strong: captain Koneru Humpy leads a squad featuring R Vaishali, Divya Deshmukh, Vantika Agrawal and Savitha Shri B.

History, however, is against a repeat. No country has successfully defended the Open title since Armenia won consecutive Olympiads in 2006 and 2008. The last five editions have produced four different champions: China in 2014 and 2018, the United States in 2016, Uzbekistan in 2022 and India in 2024.

What to watch

The immediate question is whether the accommodation mess leaves India's players rested and ready for round one on Wednesday. Beyond the logistics, the tournament poses a sporting question: can a young squad — its average age barely out of the teens for several boards — handle the pressure of defending a title that the last two decades suggest is nearly impossible to retain? The first move, at least, will not be made on the board.
image_caption: Indian grandmasters at the chessboard during a tournament. The Indian contingent was stranded for five hours on arrival in Samarkand after their hotel rooms were not allotted.
nri_angle: Indian chess is a diaspora pride story — Gukesh's world title and the 2024 double gold made the team a household name among Indian families abroad, who follow the Olympiad closely.
